source.title: SEDATE: Do Large Language Models Share an Aggression Circuit Across Languages?
source.authors: Sagnik Basu; Sayan Das; Somnath Banerjee; Animesh Mukherjee

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some tables are flattened or have ambiguous column alignment.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses selected neurons as detectors and intervention targets, then reports performance of its own method. It does not test the claim versions about neuron interpretability, explanation accuracy, or attribution graphs.
record.gate_note: The paper reports finding a cross-lingual aggression-neuron core and measures changes in its aggression signal after intervention. Safety-score and general-capability results are not included as rows because none of the listed claim versions names those outcomes. It does not test explanations on held-out activations or report shares of neurons by number of jobs.
record.test_reason: The study selects aggression-sensitive FFN neurons by an entropy score and uses them as a detector and intervention target for safety steering. It reports its own method's safety and capability performance. It never assigns jobs to neurons, reports shares of interpretable neurons, scores explanations by simulation, analyzes vision neurons, or builds attribution graphs. So no version is tested. The neurons-as-intervention-target result is related but does not measure what V5 names: attribution graphs explaining behaviour versus a replacement model.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors conclude that a cross-lingual set of aggression-responsive neurons suggests a largely language-invariant circuit, and that a small shared set of neurons can serve as both detector and intervention target. They report that SEDATE beats the baselines and retains general capabilities, except for ROUGE drops on CNN/DM. It generalizes to 4 unseen languages and 4 datasets.
record.recipe_differences: The paper selects aggression-sensitive neurons using AAPE and cross-language overlap, then conditionally suppresses and steers activations. It does not use the original audit’s neuron-pole job descriptions or test held-out explanations.
record.method_sensitivity: The aggression signal and neuron selection are defined from language-specific corpora; the study describes calibration of thresholds and intervention strength, but does not report these as changing the interpretability claims in the versions.

fits_no_version.finding: An intersection of entropy-selected aggression-sensitive FFN neurons across seven languages is reported. Its size is not given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some FFN neurons in 7B–9B LLMs fire selectively on aggressive content across multiple languages.

fits_no_version.finding: Suppressing these neurons and steering the residual stream shrinks the aggressive-minus-benign signal gap, to near zero for the Mistral models. It also reduces the external safety cost, with ROUGE drops of up to about 7.6 points on CNN/DM.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Selected individual neurons can serve as effective intervention targets for a behaviour, at some cost on benign text about violence.

record.problems: The paper does not report numerical core-set sizes or per-language/model CLAO values, and the signal-gap discussion gives qualitative results rather than exact values for each condition. Human evaluation uses 10 prompts per language. Some table text is flattened or ambiguous, and the text contains internal inconsistencies such as references to six models where the paper otherwise describes seven.
record.rows_left_out: Safety-score, unsafe-rate, judge-comparison, and general-capability results were left out because they do not measure any outcome named by the claim versions. No exact Figure 2 values were extracted where only plotted values are available.

untested.parts: No audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles and no shares of neurons with one job, two jobs or unexplained jobs.
No shares of interpretable neurons in any model (7B–9B Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Aya). No MoE or scale comparison.
No InceptionV1 or vision neurons. No analysis of pose or recursive generalization.
No comparison of architecture, regularization or tool quality against interpretability share.
No attribution graphs, no replacement-model comparison, no reconstruction error.
No test of whether explanations from activating examples predict held-out activations. Neuron selection is by corpus-level firing probability, not by explanations.
No simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The models are 7 (Llama, Mistral and Qwen base and instruct, plus Aya-instruct), although some passages say six models or three families. The study cites 'features grow monosemantic at scale' only in passing. Neuron interpretability shares are never measured, so it does not bear on any version.

versions.untested_parts: Does not audit Qwen3-32B neuron poles, assign human-readable jobs, or report the stated shares.
Does not measure one-job/two-job/unexplained shares across models or scale; its cross-lingual neuron-set result is about aggression selection, not those shares.
Does not analyze InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose, or recursive generalization.
Does not test architecture, regularization, tool quality, or the stated InceptionV1-sized vision-model estimates.
Does not build or evaluate attribution graphs, compare against a trained replacement model, or report reconstruction error.
Does not test whether explanations fit activating examples but fail to predict activations on new examples.
Does not score neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

rows.subject: all evaluated models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compute language-specific aggression-sensitive neuron sets and their cross-lingual overlap/core.

conditions.value: 7 evaluated languages: English, French, German, Spanish, Italian, Chinese, Japanese

rows.value: The authors report finding a cross-lingual set of neurons responding to aggression across all evaluated languages.
rows.note: The paper does not give core-set sizes or numerical CLAO values in the reported text.
rows.check: This records the existence of a selected cross-lingual neuron intersection. No core-set size or CLAO values are reported, and the intersection is a selection result rather than a measured share of neurons with one job. 'observed' is only the authors' qualitative claim, so the state cannot be read numerically.

rows.subject: all evaluated models (aggregate statement)
rows.operation_detail: Compare the monitored aggression-signal gap on unmodified and intervened forward passes.

conditions.value: raw first pass versus SEDATE-intervened second pass

rows.measure: Mean aggression-signal gap between aggressive and non-aggressive inputs
rows.baseline: Before intervention, positive for every model and language, ranging from roughly 0.04 to 0.10.
rows.value: After intervention, the gap shrinks substantially in every case.
rows.locator: Discussion, “Effect of SEDATE on the aggression signal”; Figure 2
rows.note: The paper gives the range and qualitative change in text, but not exact post-intervention values for each model and language.
rows.check: This measures the study's own intervention effect on its own monitored signal, so it is a method-performance outcome. Figure 2 covers seven models, while the text says six. Post-intervention values are only plotted.
